title: Hence: premotion in Eden for the Thomists, not for Jansenius
source_text: LXXVII. Ac proinde, secundum Thomistarum hypotheses, auxilium physice praedeterminans necessarium fuit, homini etiam integro, & citra ullam peccati considerationem. Sed juxta Jansenium, adjutorium efficax, quo fit ut homo velit & operetur, nullum locum habuit in statu innocentiae; Sed solum adjutorium sine quo homo quidem bene agere non poterat; & cum quo poterat facile consistere, ut homo bene non ageret; Utpote quod libero arbitrio subdebatur, minime vero liberum hominis arbitrium sibi subjiciebat.
pass_a_gloss: LXXVII. And therefore, according to the Thomists' hypotheses, the help physically predetermining was necessary, to man even unfallen, and apart from any consideration of sin. But according to Jansenius, the efficacious help, by which it comes about that man wills and works, had no place in the state of innocence; But only the help without which man indeed could not act well; and with which it could easily stand, that man did not act well; Inasmuch as it was subjected to free choice, but by no means subjected the free choice of man to itself.
pass_b_english: Thesis LXXVII. On the Thomists' assumptions, then, the physically predetermining aid was necessary even for man unfallen, quite apart from any thought of sin. On Jansenius's view, by contrast, the efficacious aid by which a person comes to will and act had no place in the state of innocence.

There was only the aid without which man could not act well, and which could easily coexist with his not acting well, since it was subject to free choice and in no way brought man's free choice under itself.
